Still, the material collected in the classical Arabic dictionaries, together with what we find in works on Qur’anic interpretation, hadith, Qur’anic readings, the Prophet’s campaigns, the “Battle Days of the Arabs,” Arab stories, collections of pre-Islamic poetry and their commentaries, and the poetic and linguistic examples preserved in works of grammar, gives us a rich and important body of evidence.
This material can support a scientific study capable of clearing away some of the uncertainty surrounding the life of Arabic during this stage in the development of Arab society.
From this large and varied body of material, we can begin with the following conclusions.

The first conclusion is that the classical Arabic preserved for us in the Qur’an, hadith, poetry attributed to the pre-Islamic period, and the various forms of artistic prose attributed to pre-Islamic Arabs and the earliest Muslims—including the Companions and the Rightly Guided Caliphs—was a common linguistic form in which the dialects of the northern Arabs, together with some southern dialects, had blended and come together.

We have plenty of evidence that the same historical conditions that gave Mecca its special and influential position in trade, economic life, society, and religion also made the dialect of Quraysh a center of attraction where other Arabic dialects, especially the northern ones, met and influenced one another.
During the sixth century CE, this interaction and blending must gradually have produced a shared form of Arabic distinct from the local dialects.

It became the language of artistic expression in poetry, public speaking, and short sayings of wisdom. It also became a shared language of communication among the different tribes when they came together at seasonal gatherings for trade, religion, and literature.
This kind of unification did not make the different dialects disappear.

Each Arab community continued to use its own dialect in ordinary everyday speech. At the same time, people could understand and use the common language when they met others at the great seasonal markets and gatherings.
Ibn Hishām may have been describing precisely this unity within diversity when he wrote:
“The Arabs would recite one another’s poetry, while each spoke according to the natural speech he had grown up with. This is why so many different versions of the same verses arose.”
This movement toward linguistic unity did not take place separately from the economic, social, cultural, and religious changes taking place in pre-Islamic society.

It was part of the wider development of that society toward new kinds of social relationships. Economic connections were beginning to bind its different parts together, gradually moving it away from tribal fragmentation and toward greater social unity.
This new unity was itself developing within a framework of growing social differences that would eventually provide the material basis for class divisions.

Language certainly has a degree of independence from a society’s economic foundations and from its wider social, political, and cultural structures. But that independence is never complete. Language does not exist outside the history of society, because it does not exist outside society itself.
Arabic therefore had to be affected by one of the most important changes taking place at the time: the movement away from tribal fragmentation and toward greater social unity.
This is why the dialect of Quraysh became the main basis of the developing common language.

The Qurayshi dialect did not become dominant because of some special quality contained in the dialect itself. Its influence came from the economic, commercial, social, and religious position of the Meccan Qurayshi aristocracy and from the influence that this position gave them over the wider course of social development.
The northern Arab communities increasingly had to deal with this aristocracy through its dialect rather than through their own separate dialects.

As a result, the dialect of Quraysh spread widely. This in turn allowed it to absorb useful features from other dialects. The process enriched its vocabulary and meanings and gave it a greater ability to bring different dialects together into a common language.
This was an objective historical process. It was not the result of deliberate personal choice or conscious selection.
Al-Farrāʾ imagined the matter differently when he wrote:

“The Arabs used to attend the seasonal gathering each year and make the pilgrimage to the House in the pre-Islamic period. Quraysh would hear the different ways the Arabs spoke. Whatever they liked in their speech, they adopted. In this way they became the most eloquent of the Arabs, and their language became free of ugly forms of speech and unpleasant words.”
But the process was not a matter of deliberate “preference.”
It was the natural result of the wider conditions to which al-Farrāʾ himself refers in the first part of this passage.

We can see the result most clearly in the fact that a poet who did not belong to Quraysh would avoid the special features of his own dialect—its particular ways of forming words, pronouncing sounds, and building sentences—in order to address people in a language they already knew and accepted.
Many different forces had helped refine and polish this common language.

The two conclusions above make it much easier to explain why the dialect of Quraysh, rather than any other Arabic dialect, became both the material and the subject of the linguistic studies developed by Muslim scholars from the beginning of the age of systematic writing and authorship in Arabic.
It might be argued that Muslim scholars gave so much attention to the language of Quraysh simply because it was the language of the Qur’an.
From this point of view, their interest was religious rather than historical.
There is some truth in this, and it must be taken seriously. But it does not cancel out the other side of the question: the objective historical side. In fact, it confirms it.
The fact that the language of Quraysh became the language of the Qur’an was itself part of this historical process.
That remains true whatever religious motives guided scholars of Qur’anic interpretation and hadith, or scholars of language, grammar, literature, and rhetoric.

The same historical conditions that had already established the language of Quraysh as a common form of Arabic also explain why the Islamic message, in both Qur’an and hadith, addressed the Arabs in a language they already knew and shared.
There is no doubt that becoming the language of the Qur’an and hadith then strengthened the movement toward linguistic unity even further.

It also broadened the direct meanings of words, expanded the language’s figurative and expressive possibilities, and developed its ability to express the new ideas about the universe, society, and law that came with the changes of the Islamic period.
But we should also remember that linguistic studies did not remain entirely dependent on the study of the Qur’an and hadith.
Some branches gradually began to study questions of Arabic as subjects in their own right, becoming increasingly independent of their original religious purpose.

The earliest reasons for studying grammar were certainly connected with the need to establish rules for the grammatical forms of Qur’anic Arabic. Scholars did this partly by examining grammatical patterns in texts attributed to the pre-Islamic Arabs.

But despite these beginnings, the study of grammar gradually developed a life of its own. Its subject and purpose expanded, and specialist scholars emerged who wanted to study the Arabic language as a whole.
They began to study grammar for its own sake, not simply as part of the work of studying the Qur’an.
In this section, we look at pre-Islamic poetry—or rather, at the part of it that has reached us in written form—from a historical point of view.
Our concern here is with poetry as a historical, cultural, and social feature of late pre-Islamic Arab society.
We have no doubt that, in this respect, pre-Islamic poetry has a special value. Both its style and its content preserve vivid features of that society.
Its language, style, meter, subjects, descriptive images, and social images all contribute to this value.

The very existence of this poetry, with all these features, during such an important stage of Arab history before Islam makes it an important document. For scientific research, it is one of the richest, most varied, and most wide-ranging historical sources available to us.
But the scientific study of pre-Islamic poetry faces two problems that require a sound method of investigation.

Unless we find such a method, our use of this poetry as historical evidence will remain limited, and we will be able to draw only a small part of the scientific information and conclusions it may contain.

A large amount of the poetry still classified as pre-Islamic has been questioned, both in earlier centuries and in modern times. There are even judgments close to certainty that much of this material was falsely attributed to the pre-Islamic period during later Islamic times and has no genuine basis for being dated that early.
The second problem is that all of this poetry has reached us in an apparently complete and finished form.
We cannot see the stages through which it developed.
To this day, we know almost nothing about the path by which it grew and changed before reaching the finished form known to us.
As Krachkovsky put it, we see only the static side of this poetry, not its dynamic side.
This second problem casts a shadow over the first and makes the question of authenticity even harder to solve.
Because we do not know the history of how pre-Islamic poetry developed, we have lost an important tool for deciding what is genuine: comparison.

Ideally, we would compare the poems recorded during the Islamic period with earlier examples from the stages through which this poetry must have passed as it developed during the century and a half before the rise of Islam.
If the historical conditions for such a comparison existed, it could settle the argument over whether the surviving poems really belong to the pre-Islamic period.

If we had a clear picture of pre-Islamic poetry as it grew, changed, developed its techniques, and responded to changing historical conditions over what must have been a long history, the different stages of that development would give us a strict standard of comparison.
We could then distinguish much more precisely between poems that genuinely belong to the pre-Islamic period and poems that were later placed there falsely.
But because we still lack that historical picture, we also lack this reliable standard.
The problem is much the same as the one we faced when discussing the historical development of classical Arabic.
There too, we first encounter the language in an apparently complete and finished form, in the Qur’an and in pre-Islamic poetry as it was recorded during the Islamic centuries.

As we explained earlier when discussing the linguistic dimension, the final answer to that problem must await new discoveries of written evidence in Arabia—assuming Arab scientific institutions undertake the necessary archaeological work.
For now, the question of pre-Islamic poetry can only be settled decisively by similar discoveries.

The few written remains found in Arabia so far, which we discussed earlier, cannot help us at all with the question of pre-Islamic poetry. They belong to historical conditions different from those in which pre-Islamic Arabic poetry must have arisen and developed.
Still, waiting for new discoveries does not mean we have reached a dead end.
However uncertain the possibilities may be, we do not have to stop studying the problem until new evidence appears.
Other methods of investigation remain available to us.
One useful approach is to examine the foundations of the problem itself, together with the methods and investigations that have so far been used to deal with it.
We will therefore turn to this alternative path and discuss it as far as our present purpose requires.
The historical basis for doubt begins with one firmly established fact.

The poetry composed during the pre-Islamic period continued to circulate only through memory and oral transmission until the age when it was systematically written down, in the third and fourth Islamic centuries.
In other words, for a long period it was not preserved in writing.

This meant, first, that a great deal of it was bound to disappear. Poems were scattered among different tribes and places, often far apart. The people who had memorized them also died out from one generation to the next.
Second, the wording of the poems was bound to change as they passed from one person to another and from one place to another. Sometimes this happened deliberately, and sometimes unintentionally.
When systematic recording finally began, these two factors meant that the collectors could naturally recover only a small part of the original body of poetry.
What survived had already passed through roughly two centuries after the rise of Islam during which poems could be lost, altered, or distorted.
The disappearance of so much genuine pre-Islamic poetry also deprived us of a standard by which to distinguish authentic texts from invented ones.
This alone gives us reasonable grounds for questioning whether all the poems later written down and attributed to pre-Islamic poets really belong to them.
There is another factor as well.

During the Islamic centuries, both before and after poetry began to be systematically recorded, religious, political, and social interests sometimes encouraged different groups to invent poems and attribute them to the pre-Islamic period.

Linguists, scholars of Qur’anic interpretation and hadith, transmitters of poetry, supporters of rulers, and supporters of religious or political schools could all have reasons to produce such poetry.
A fabricated poem might be used to support a religious opinion or a sectarian position, defend a political cause, or strengthen the claims of a particular tribe.
This is a historical reality that cannot simply be denied.
Once we take it into account, the historical basis for doubting the authenticity of some recorded pre-Islamic poetry becomes even stronger.
It seems that the question of whether all recorded pre-Islamic poetry was authentic was already present in the minds of early Arab and Muslim writers on literature and literary history.

Their books contain many references to different forms of poetic fabrication during the Islamic period and to poems that were falsely attributed to pre-Islamic times for the kinds of reasons just discussed.
